{{Short description|Geometrical figure in a Euclidean space}}
[[File:Eutactic star 3D.png|thumb|right|A eutactic star consisting of 5 pairs of vectors in three-dimensional space (''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;3, ''s''&nbsp;=&nbsp;5)]]
In [[Euclidean geometry]], a '''eutactic star''' is a [[geometrical figure]] in a [[Euclidean space]]. A star is a figure consisting of any number of opposing pairs of [[Euclidean vector|vector]]s (or arms) issuing from a central origin. A star is eutactic if it is the [[orthogonal]] [[projection (mathematics)|projection]] of plus and minus the set of [[standard basis]] vectors (i.e., the vertices of a [[cross-polytope]]) from a higher-dimensional space onto a [[Euclidean subspace|subspace]]. Such stars were called "eutactic" – meaning "well-situated" or "well-arranged" –  by {{harvtxt |Schläfli|1901|loc=p. 134}} because, for a common [[Scalar (mathematics)|scalar multiple]], their vectors are projections of an [[orthonormal basis]].<ref>{{cite book|title=Eigenspaces of graphs|author=D. M. Cvetković|author2=P. Rowlinson|author3=S. Simić|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=1997|isbn=0-521-57352-1|page=[https://archive.org/details/eigenspacesofgra0000cvet/page/151 151]|url=https://archive.org/details/eigenspacesofgra0000cvet/page/151}}</ref>

== Definition ==
[[File:Eutactic star.png|thumb|right|A eutactic star in the plane (''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2, ''s''&nbsp;=&nbsp;4)]]
A ''star'' is here defined as a set of 2''s'' vectors ''A''&nbsp;=&nbsp;±'''a'''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ±'''a'''<sub>''s''</sub> issuing from a particular origin in a Euclidean space of dimension ''n''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''s''.  A star is eutactic if the '''a'''<sub>''i''</sub> are the projections onto ''n'' dimensions of a set of mutually [[perpendicular]] equal vectors '''b'''<sub>1</sub>, ..., '''b'''<sub>''s''</sub> issuing from a particular origin in Euclidean ''s''-dimensional space.<ref name="Coxeter">{{cite book|title=Regular polytopes|url=https://archive.org/details/regularpolytopes0000coxe|url-access=registration|last1=Coxeter | first1=Harold Scott MacDonald | author1-link=Harold Scott MacDonald Coxeter |publisher=Courier Dover Publications|year=1973|isbn=0-486-61480-8|page=[https://archive.org/details/regularpolytopes0000coxe/page/251 251]}}</ref> The configuration of 2''s'' vectors in the ''s''-dimensional space ''B''&nbsp;=&nbsp;±'''b'''<sub>1</sub>,&nbsp;...&nbsp;, ±'''b'''<sub>''s''</sub> is known as a ''cross''.  Given these definitions, a eutactic star is, concisely, a star produced by the orthogonal projection of a cross.

An equivalent definition, first mentioned by [[Schläfli]],<ref name="Schläfli">{{Cite book | last1=Schläfli | first1=Ludwig | title=Collected mathematical works | publisher=Birkhäuser Verlag | language=German | year=1949 | volume=I | chapter=Theorie der vielfachen Kontinuität|zbl=0035.21902 }}
</ref> stipulates that a star is eutactic if a constant ''ζ'' exists such that 

:<math>\sum_{k=1}^s(\mathbf{a}_k \cdot \mathbf{v})^2 = \zeta |\mathbf{v}|^2</math>

for every vector '''v'''.  The existence of such a constant requires that the sum of the squares of the orthogonal projections of ''A''  on a line be equal in all directions.<ref name="Canada">{{Cite journal | doi=10.4153/CJM-1951-045-8 | last1=Coxeter | first1=Harold Scott MacDonald | author1-link=Harold Scott MacDonald Coxeter | title=Extreme forms | mr=0044580 | year=1951 | journal=Canadian Journal of Mathematics| issn=0008-414X | volume=3 | pages=391–441 | s2cid=247197697 | doi-access=free }}</ref> In general, 
:<math>\zeta = \sum_{k=1}^s |\mathbf{a}_k|^2/n.</math>

A ''normalised'' eutactic star is a projected cross composed of [[unit vector]]s.<ref name="Coxeter" /><ref>{{cite web|url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/EutacticStar.html|title=Eutactic Star – MathWorld|author=E. W. Weisstein|accessdate=2009-08-28}}</ref>  Eutactic stars are often considered in ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;3 dimensions because of their connection with the study of [[regular polyhedra]].

==Hadwiger's principal theorem==
Let ''T'' be the [[symmetric matrix|symmetric]] [[linear transformation]] defined for vectors '''x''' by
:<math>T\mathbf{x} = \sum_{k=1}^s \mathbf{a}_k (\mathbf{a}_k\cdot\mathbf{x}),</math>
where the '''a'''<sub>''j''</sub> form any collection of ''s'' vectors in the ''n''-dimensional Euclidean space. [[Hadwiger]]'s principal theorem states that the vectors ±'''a'''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ±'''a'''<sub>''s''</sub> form a eutactic star [[if and only if]] there is a constant ''ζ'' such that ''T'''''x''' = ''ζ'''''x''' for every '''x'''.<ref name="Coxeter" /><ref>{{cite web|url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/HadwigersPrincipalTheorem.html|title=Hadwiger's Principal Theorem – MathWorld|author=E. W. Weisstein|accessdate=2009-08-28}}</ref>  The vectors form a normalized eutactic star precisely when ''T'' is the [[identity operator]] – when ''ζ''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1.

Equivalently, the star is normalized eutactic if and only if the [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]]  '''A'''&nbsp;=&nbsp;['''a'''<sub>1</sub> ... '''a'''<sub>''s''</sub>], whose columns are the vectors '''a'''<sub>''k''</sub>, has [[orthonormal]] rows.  A proof may be given in one direction by completing the rows of this matrix to an [[orthonormal basis]] of <math>\mathbb{R}^s</math>, and in the other by orthogonally projecting onto the ''n''-dimensional subspace spanned by the first ''n'' Cartesian coordinate vectors.

[[Hadwiger's theorem]] implies the equivalence of Schläfli's stipulation and the geometrical definition of a eutactic star, by the [[polarization identity]].  Furthermore, both Schläfli's identity and Hadwiger's theorem give the same value of the constant&nbsp;''ζ''.

== Applications ==

Eutactic stars are useful largely because of their relationship with the geometry of [[polytope]]s and [[group (mathematics)|groups]] of [[orthogonal transformation]]s.  Schläfli showed early on that the vectors from the center of any [[regular polytope]] to its vertices form a eutactic star.  Brauer and Coxeter proved the following generalization:<ref>{{Cite journal | last1=Brauer | first1=R. | author1-link=Richard Brauer | last2=Coxeter | first2=Harold Scott MacDonald | author2-link=Harold Scott MacDonald Coxeter | title=A generalization of theorems of Schönhardt and Mehmke on polytopes | mr=0002869 | year=1940 | journal=Trans. Roy. Soc. Canada. Sect. III. (3) | volume=34 | pages=29–34 }}.</ref>

:<blockquote>A star is eutactic if it is transformed to itself by some irreducible group of orthogonal transformations that acts transitively on pairs of opposite vectors.</blockquote>

An irreducible group here means a group that does not leave any nontrivial proper subspace invariant (see [[irreducible representation]]). Since the set theoretic union of two eutactic stars is itself eutactic (a consequence of [[#Hadwiger's principal theorem|Hadwiger's principal theorem]]), it can be concluded that, in general:<ref name="Canada" />
:<blockquote>A star is eutactic if it is transformed to itself by some irreducible group of orthogonal transformations.</blockquote>

Eutactic stars may be used to validate the eutaxy of any form in general. According to [[H. S. M. Coxeter]]: "A form is eutactic if and only if its minimal vectors are [[parallel (geometry)|parallel]] to the vectors of a eutactic star."<ref name="Canada" />
